verifications.claim: Measles is caused by the measles virus.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Measles is caused by a virus" (R1); "Measles is a contagious viral disease" (R2); "caused by the measles virus" (R9)
verifications.reasoning: Multiple sources directly state measles is caused by the measles virus.

verifications.claim: Measles spreads through airborne droplets.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "droplets spray into the air" (R1); "spreads when someone infected speaks, coughs, sneezes or breathes" (R2); "spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes" (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Sources explicitly describe spread via airborne droplets from coughing, sneezing, etc.

verifications.claim: Measles spreads through coughing, sneezing, or close contact.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "coughs, sneezes or talks, droplets spray into the air" (R1); "speaks, coughs, sneezes or breathes" (R2); "coughs or sneezes" (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Direct support for coughing and sneezing; close contact via droplets or surfaces implied and stated.

verifications.claim: The measles virus can live in the air or on surfaces for up to 2 hours.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "droplets can infect other people for up to two hours" (R1); "linger in the air up to two hours" (R2); "up to 2 hours after that person has left" (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Exact phrasing in multiple sources confirms virus viability up to 2 hours in air or on surfaces.

verifications.claim: Infected people can spread the measles virus 4 days before to 4 days after the rash appears.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "four days before the rash appears and four days after" (R1); "four days before their rash starts to four days afterwards" (R2); "from four days before through four days after the rash appears" (R3)
verifications.reasoning: Precise timeframe directly matches across sources.

verifications.claim: Symptoms typically appear 7–14 days after exposure to measles.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "around 7 to 14 days after contact with the virus" (R1); "Measles symptoms appear 7 to 14 days after contact with the virus" (R4); "7 to 14 days after exposure" (R13)
verifications.reasoning: Exact incubation period stated directly.

verifications.claim: Initial symptoms of measles include high fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Fever... Dry cough. Runny nose. Red, watering eyes" (R1); "High fever... Cough Runny nose... Red, watery eyes" (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Lists exact initial symptoms verbatim.

verifications.claim: Initial symptoms of measles include conjunctivitis.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Red, watering eyes, called conjunctivitis" (R1); "Conjunctivitis (pink eye)" (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Directly names conjunctivitis as initial symptom.

verifications.claim: Small white spots known as Koplik spots may appear inside the cheeks as early signs of measles.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "tiny white spots inside the mouth, called Koplik spots" (R1); "Koplik's spots... inside the mouth" (R6)
verifications.reasoning: Precise description and name match.

verifications.claim: The measles rash is red and blotchy.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "blotchy rash... shades of red" (R1); "flat red spots" (R6); "rash of red spots" (R11)
verifications.reasoning: Directly described as blotchy and red in sources.

verifications.claim: The measles rash appears 3-5 days after initial symptoms.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "About 3 to 5 days after symptoms first start" (R1); "The rash breaks out 3–5 days after symptoms start" (R6)
verifications.reasoning: Exact timing matches.

verifications.claim: The measles rash starts on the face and spreads downward.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "starts on the face or neck and spreads down the body" (R1); "appears on the face... Then it affects the rest of the body" (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Consistent description of rash progression.

verifications.claim: The measles rash lasts 5-6 days.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "It usually lasts 5–6 days before fading" (R7)
verifications.reasoning: Directly stated in WHO source.

verifications.claim: Common complications of measles include ear infections and severe diarrhea.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Ear infection. One of the most common complications"; "Diarrhea and vomiting" (R1); "Common complications are ear infections and diarrhea" (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Explicitly listed as common.

verifications.claim: Severe complications of measles include pneumonia.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Pneumonia. Measles can cause an infection in the lungs" (R1); "Pneumonia" (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Widely cited as severe complication.

verifications.claim: Severe complications of measles include encephalitis.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Encephalitis. About 1 in 1,000 people with measles" (R1); "Encephalitis (brain swelling)" (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Consistently listed as severe.

verifications.claim: Severe complications of measles include death.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "even deadly" (R1); "Sometimes death" (R2); "leading to complications and even death" (R3)
verifications.reasoning: Death directly stated as possible severe outcome.

verifications.claim: Pneumonia is a common cause of death from measles.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Pneumonia and encephalitis complications are the most common causes of death from measles" (R1); "Pneumonia... is the most common cause of measles-related death" (R10)
verifications.reasoning: Explicitly identified as common cause of death.

verifications.claim: Measles can cause severe complications like pneumonia and encephalitis, especially in children under 5.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "especially true for children younger than age 5" (R1); "especially in children younger than 5 years of age" (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Specific complications and high-risk group match.

verifications.claim: High-risk groups for measles complications include children under 5.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "children younger than age 5" (R1); "children younger than 5 years of age" (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Directly listed as high-risk.

verifications.claim: High-risk groups for measles complications include adults over 20.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Adults older than age 20" (R1); "adults over age 30" (R7)
verifications.reasoning: Matches high-risk group description.

verifications.claim: High-risk groups for measles complications include pregnant individuals.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "People who are pregnant" (R1); "especially in... pregnant people" (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Explicitly stated as high-risk.

verifications.claim: High-risk groups for measles complications include those with weakened immune systems.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "people with severely weakened immune systems" (R1); "weak immune system" (R7)
verifications.reasoning: Consistently identified as high-risk.

verifications.claim: The Measles-Mumps-Rubella (MMR) vaccine is 97% effective.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "the vaccine gives lifelong protection... for about 97% of people who get two doses" (R1); "Two doses provide 97% protection" (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Exact effectiveness rate for MMR (two doses) stated.

verifications.claim: There is no specific antiviral treatment for measles.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "treated by managing symptoms" (R1); "no specific medical treatment for it" (R6); "no specific treatment for measles" (R7)
verifications.reasoning: Sources confirm no specific antiviral, only supportive care.

verifications.claim: Vaccination is the only effective preventative measure against measles.
verifications.label: VAGUE
verifications.evidence: "A vaccine can prevent measles infection" (R1); "The best protection against measles is... MMR vaccine" (R4); "Being vaccinated is the best way" (R7)
verifications.reasoning: Sources emphasize vaccine as best/most effective prevention, but mention post-exposure options like IG, making 'only' slightly broader.

verifications.claim: As of March 2026, over 1,400 measles cases have been reported in the US this year.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "As of March 26, 2026, 1,575 confirmed measles cases were reported in the United States in 2026"
verifications.reasoning: CDC data confirms over 1,400 cases as of late March 2026.
